claim: Drosophila type II neuroblast lineages are prone to developing impaired neuroblast homeostasis if the limited self-renewing potential of intermediate neural progenitors (INPs) is unrestrained.
source: Drosophila type II neuroblast lineages are prone to developing impaired neuroblast homeostasis if the limited self-renewing potential of intermediate neural progenitors (INPs) is unrestrained.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known characteristic of type II neuroblast lineages, drawing from established scientific knowledge about these cell types.

claim: Drosophila SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling Brahma (Brm) complex functions cooperatively with Histone deacetylase 3 (HDAC3) to suppress the formation of ectopic type II neuroblasts.
source: Here, we demonstrate that Drosophila SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling Brahma (Brm) complex functions cooperatively with another chromatin remodeling factor, Histone deacetylase 3 (HDAC3) to suppress the formation of ectopic type II neuroblasts.
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated through experimental data presented in the manuscript, including genetic interaction studies and phenotypic analyses.

claim: Multiple components of the Brm complex and HDAC3 physically associate with Earmuff (Erm).
source: We show that multiple components of the Brm complex and HDAC3 physically associate with Earmuff (Erm), a type II-specific transcription factor that prevents dedifferentiation of INPs into neuroblasts.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation and protein pull-down assays shown in Figure 4.

claim: The predicted Erm-binding motif is present in most of known binding loci of Brm.
source: Consistently, the predicted Erm-binding motif is present in most of known binding loci of Brm.
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis described in the manuscript showing that 202 out of 270 Brm binding sites contain the predicted Erm-binding motif.

claim: brm and hdac3 genetically interact with erm to prevent type II neuroblast overgrowth.
source: Furthermore, brm and hdac3 genetically interact with erm to prevent type II neuroblast overgrowth.
evidence: This is demonstrated through genetic interaction experiments showing enhanced phenotypes when these genes are simultaneously knocked down.

claim: The Brm-HDAC3-Erm repressor complex suppresses dedifferentiation of INPs back into type II neuroblasts.
source: Thus, the Brm-HDAC3-Erm repressor complex suppresses dedifferentiation of INPs back into type II neuroblasts.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the physical association data, genetic interaction data, and phenotypic analyses presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: In Drosophila larval central brains, there are at least two classes of neuroblast lineages.
source: In Drosophila larval central brains, there are at least two classes of neuroblast lineages (Bello et al., 2008; Boone and Doe, 2008; Bowman et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous publications.

claim: A type I neuroblast expresses both Deadpan (Dpn) and Asense (Ase).
source: A type I neuroblast that expresses both Deadpan (Dpn) and Asense (Ase) divides asymmetrically to generate a self-renewing neuroblast and a ganglion mother cell (GMC), which is committed to a differentiation pathway.
evidence: This is established knowledge about type I neuroblasts cited from the literature.

claim: A type II neuroblast expresses Dpn, but not Ase.
source: In contrast, a type II neuroblast that expresses Dpn, but not Ase, divides asymmetrically to generate a neuroblast and a transient amplifying cell known as an intermediate neural progenitor (INP) (Bello et al., 2008; Boone and Doe, 2008; Bowman et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge about type II neuroblasts cited from the literature.

claim: Following maturation, the INP undergoes a limited number of asymmetric divisions to self-renew and to produce multiple GMCs.
source: Following maturation, the INP undergoes a limited number of asymmetric divisions to self-renew and to produce multiple GMCs (Weng et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The failure of asymmetric division in either type of neuroblast can result in the hyperproliferation of these cells and the induction of brain tumors.
source: The failure of asymmetric division in either type of neuroblast can result in the hyperproliferation of these cells and the induction of brain tumors (Caussinus and Gonzalez, 2005; Wang et al., 2006, 2007, 2009, 2011; Lee et al., 2006a, 2006b; Cabernard and Doe, 2009; Chabu and Doe, 2009, 2011; Chang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous publications.

claim: The type II neuroblast lineage is highly analogous to the mammalian neural stem cell lineages, because both involve transient amplifying cells that are used to expand the progenitor cell population.
source: The type II neuroblast lineage is highly analogous to the mammalian neural stem cell lineages, because both involve transient amplifying cells that are used to expand the progenitor cell population.
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on established knowledge about both systems.

claim: Brain tumor (Brat) and the Notch antagonist Numb function cooperatively to ensure that immature INPs undergo maturation and commit to the INP fate.
source: Brain tumor (Brat) and the Notch antagonist Numb function cooperatively to ensure that immature INPs undergo maturation and commit to the INP fate (Boone and Doe, 2008; Bowman et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous publications.

claim: Notch signaling maintains neuroblast identity and its overactivation leads to dedifferentiation of INPs to ectopic neuroblasts.
source: Notch signaling maintains neuroblast identity and its overactivation leads to dedifferentiation of INPs to ectopic neuroblasts (Wang et al., 2006; Bowman et al., 2008; Weng et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous publications.

claim: Earmuff (Erm) is specifically expressed in INPs and plays a critical role in maintaining the restricted developmental potential of the INPs.
source: Specifically expressed in INPs, a Zinc-finger transcription factor Earmuff (Erm) plays a critical role in maintaining the restricted developmental potential of the INPs (Weng et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The Ets transcription factor Pointed (PntP1) is specifically expressed in type II neuroblasts and INPs and is both necessary and sufficient for the suppression of Ase in type II neuroblasts and the generation of INPs.
source: The Ets transcription factor Pointed (PntP1) is specifically expressed in type II neuroblasts and INPs and is both necessary and sufficient for the suppression of Ase in type II neuroblasts and the generation of INPs (Zhu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Prospero is basally localized in mitotic type I neuroblast, but absent from type II neuroblasts, and triggers cell cycle exit and GMC differentiation.
source: Prospero that is basally localized in mitotic type I neuroblast, but absent from type II neuroblasts, triggers cell cycle exit and GMC differentiation (Bello et al., 2006; Betschinger et al., 2006; Choksi et al., 2006; Lee et al., 2006c).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous publications.

claim: The mammalian SWI/SNF complex termed the Brahma (Brm or Brg1) complex regulates critical cellular processes such as differentiation and cell cycle arrest.
source: The mammalian SWI/SNF complex termed the Brahma (Brm or Brg1) complex regulates critical cellular processes such as differentiation and cell cycle arrest (Klochendler-Yeivin et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Drosophila Brm complex acts similarly to control cell proliferation and differentiation.
source: Drosophila Brm complex acts similarly to control cell proliferation (Brumby et al., 2002) and differentiation (Marenda et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous publications.

claim: A genome-wide RNAi study in Drosophila neuroblasts showed that the knockdown of genes encoding several core subunits of the SWI/SNF Brahma (Brm) remodeling complex may lead to neuroblast overproliferation.
source: A genome-wide RNAi study in Drosophila neuroblasts showed that the knockdown of genes encoding several core subunits of the SWI/SNF Brahma (Brm) remodeling complex may lead to neuroblast overproliferation (Neumuller et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Histone deacetylases (HDACs) remove acetyl groups from the tails of core histones in the nucleosome and are often associated with transcriptional co-repressors.
source: Histone deacetylases (HDACs) remove acetyl groups from the tails of core histones in the nucleosome and are often associated with transcriptional co-repressors (Dokmanovic et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge about HDACs supported by citation.

claim: brm RNAi knockdown in larval brains resulted in an increase of Miranda-positive neuroblast-like cells in larval central brains.
source: We independently identified brm from a RNA interference (RNAi) screen in which brm RNAi knockdown in larval brains resulted in an increase of Miranda-positive neuroblast-like cells in larval central brains (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), showing a phenotype similar to one previously reported (Neumuller et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The number of cells expressing the proto-oncogene dMyc was significantly increased upon brm RNAi knockdown.
source: The number of cells expressing the proto-oncogene dMyc was significantly increased upon brm RNAi knockdown (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), consistent with the neuroblast overgrowth phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Brm has no significant effect on type I neuroblast numbers.
source: Type I wild-type (wt) clones always contained one neuroblast that is positive for both Dpn and Ase (data not shown). Similarly, only one neuroblast was present in both amorphic brm2 and hypomorphic brmT362 type I clones (data not shown), indicating that Brm has no significant effect on type I neuroblast numbers.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations of type I neuroblast clones.

claim: Each wild-type type II MARCM clone possessed only one neuroblast that was positive for Dpn, but negative for Ase.
source: Each wt type II MARCM clone also possessed only one neuroblast that was positive for Dpn, but negative for Ase (Figure 1A; n = 25).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: 6.4 ± 3.3 ectopic neuroblasts were observed in brm2 type II clones.
source: Unlike the wt control, 6.4 ± 3.3 and 4.5 ± 2.6 ectopic neuroblasts were observed in brm2 (Figure 1B,B′,D; 88.6%, n = 34) brmT362 (Figure 1C,C′,D; 75.9%, n = 58) type II clones, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1B,B′,D.

claim: 4.5 ± 2.6 ectopic neuroblasts were observed in brmT362 type II clones.
source: Unlike the wt control, 6.4 ± 3.3 and 4.5 ± 2.6 ectopic neuroblasts were observed in brm2 (Figure 1B,B′,D; 88.6%, n = 34) brmT362 (Figure 1C,C′,D; 75.9%, n = 58) type II clones, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1C,C′,D.

claim: The phenotypes in brm alleles could be rescued by expressing a wild-type brm transgene.
source: These phenotypes in brm alleles could be rescued by expressing a wild-type brm transgene (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Knockdown of brm by RNAi using a type II neuroblast-specific driver was sufficient to produce ectopic neuroblasts in 97.4% of type II neuroblast lineages.
source: Consistent with phenotypes in brm clones, knockdown of brm by RNAi using a type II neuroblast-specific neuroblast driver worniu (wor)-Gal4, ase-Gal80 (henceforth referred to as 'type II driver'; 'Materials and methods') was sufficient to produce ectopic neuroblasts in 97.4% of type II neuroblast lineages (Figure 1F,K; 7 ± 3.4 neuroblasts/lineage, n = 38), while each control clone always has one neuroblast (Figure 1E,K; n = 80).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F,K.

claim: Brm suppresses the formation of ectopic neuroblasts in type II neuroblast lineages.
source: We therefore conclude that Brm suppresses the formation of ectopic neuroblasts in type II neuroblast lineages.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from multiple experimental observations showing ectopic neuroblasts in brm mutants and knockdowns.

claim: The number of mature INPs that are positive for Dpn and Ase were dramatically reduced in both brm2 and brmT362 compared with the control type II clones.
source: Concomitantly with the formation of supernumerary neuroblasts, the number of mature INPs that are positive for Dpn and Ase were dramatically reduced in both brm2 (Figure 2B,B′,D; 5.3 ± 4.3/clone, n = 39) and brmT362 (Figure 2C,C′,D; 9.6 ± 4.6/clone, n = 56), compared with the control type II clones (Figure 2A,A′,D; 18.9 ± 3.7, n = 22).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2B,B′,C,C′,D.

claim: The number of Dpn− PntP1+ immature INPs and early mature INPs appeared to be normal or slightly increased in brm2 and brmT362 clones compared with the control.
source: The number of Dpn− PntP1+ immature INPs and early mature INPs appeared to be normal or slightly increased in brm2 (Figure 2F; 8.4 ± 2.5, n = 26) and brmT362 (Figure 2G; 7.1 ± 2.1, n = 33) clones compared with the control (Figure 2E; 5.9 ± 1.1, n = 26).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2E,F,G.

claim: Ectopic neuroblasts in brm− clones likely originate from INPs that fail to undergo maturation.
source: These results suggested that ectopic neuroblasts in brm− clones likely originate from INPs that fail to undergo maturation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mature INPs are reduced while immature INPs are normal or increased.

claim: In 42.5% of INP clones with brm knockdown, ectopic Dpn+ Ase− neuroblasts were observed.
source: To further determine whether INPs undergo dedifferentiation back into neuroblast, we used INP-specific RNAi to knock down brm in INPs by erm-Gal4, an INP-specific driver. In 42.5% of INP clones with brm knockdown, ectopic Dpn+ Ase− neuroblasts were observed (Figure 2I,I′; 1.2 ± 1.6 neuroblasts /INP clone, n = 40).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I,I′.

claim: None of the INP clones from the driver control contained any neuroblasts.
source: In contrast, none of the INP clones from the driver control contained any neuroblasts (Figure 2H; 0 neuroblast/INP clone, n = 53).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Brm functions in INPs to prevent INP dedifferentiation back into neuroblasts.
source: Thus, our data suggest that Brm functions in INPs to prevent INP dedifferentiation back into neuroblasts.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from INP-specific knockdown experiments showing ectopic neuroblasts.

claim: brm2 MARCM clones did not show any defects in the localization of aPKC, Numb and Brat.
source: To assess whether Brm was affecting apico-basal cell polarity, we examined the localization of aPKC, Numb and Brat, which are asymmetrically localized in wild-type neuroblasts in prometaphase/metaphase. brm2 MARCM clones did not show any defects in the localization of these markers (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C), suggesting that Brm is not important for the apical-basal polarity regulation in neuroblasts.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Brm is not important for the apical-basal polarity regulation in neuroblasts.
source: brm2 MARCM clones did not show any defects in the localization of these markers (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C), suggesting that Brm is not important for the apical-basal polarity regulation in neuroblasts.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that polarity markers localize normally in brm mutants.

claim: Knock down of snr1 resulted in prominent phenotypes with ectopic Dpn+ Ase− neuroblasts in type II neuroblast lineages.
source: We then assessed the function of other core subunits of the Brm remodeling complex using RNAi knockdown in larval brains. Knock down either of the three core components snr1 (Figure 1G,K, 9.5 ± 5.5 neuroblasts/lineage, 64.5%, n = 34), bap60 (Figure 1H,K, 5.1 ± 2.8 neuroblasts/lineage, 87.0%, n = 52), and moira (data not shown; also reported in Neumuller et al. (2011)) resulted in prominent phenotypes with ectopic Dpn+ Ase− neuroblasts in type II neuroblast lineages.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G,K.

claim: Knock down of bap60 resulted in prominent phenotypes with ectopic Dpn+ Ase− neuroblasts in type II neuroblast lineages.
source: Knock down either of the three core components snr1 (Figure 1G,K, 9.5 ± 5.5 neuroblasts/lineage, 64.5%, n = 34), bap60 (Figure 1H,K, 5.1 ± 2.8 neuroblasts/lineage, 87.0%, n = 52), and moira (data not shown; also reported in Neumuller et al. (2011)) resulted in prominent phenotypes with ectopic Dpn+ Ase− neuroblasts in type II neuroblast lineages.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H,K.

claim: Knock down of moira resulted in prominent phenotypes with ectopic Dpn+ Ase− neuroblasts in type II neuroblast lineages.
source: Knock down either of the three core components snr1 (Figure 1G,K, 9.5 ± 5.5 neuroblasts/lineage, 64.5%, n = 34), bap60 (Figure 1H,K, 5.1 ± 2.8 neuroblasts/lineage, 87.0%, n = 52), and moira (data not shown; also reported in Neumuller et al. (2011)) resulted in prominent phenotypes with ectopic Dpn+ Ase− neuroblasts in type II neuroblast lineages.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to previous work.

claim: bap55LL5955 MARCM clones showed ectopic neuroblasts in type II but not type I neuroblast lineages.
source: Furthermore, bap55LL5955 MARCM clones also showed ectopic neuroblasts in type II (Figure 1J,J′, 2.3 ± 1.7 neuroblasts/clone; 30.5%, n = 57), but not type I neuroblast lineages (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F; n = 20).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1J,J′ and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The number of Dpn+ Ase+ mature INPs in bap55LL5955 was significantly reduced compared with the control.
source: The number of Dpn+ Ase+ mature INPs in bap55LL5955 was significantly reduced (13.8 ± 4.1; n = 49) compared with the control (18.9 ± 3.7, n = 22), while the number of Dpn− PntP1+ immature and early mature INPs (4.2 ± 1.9, n = 26) was similar to the control (5.9 ± 1.1, n = 26).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from the experiments.

claim: Core components of the Brm remodeling complex are required to suppress ectopic neuroblast formation in type II neuroblast lineages.
source: We conclude that core components of the Brm remodeling complex are required to suppress ectopic neuroblast formation in type II neuroblast lineages.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from multiple experiments showing ectopic neuroblasts upon loss of various Brm complex components.

claim: RNAi knockdown of nurf301, iswi, or acf1 in the type II neuroblast lineages did not result in any obvious neuroblast overgrowth.
source: Next, we ascertained whether other chromatin remodeling complexes such as Nucleosome remodeling factor (NURF) and ACF complex (ATP-utilizing chromatin assembly and remodeling factor), play any role during neuroblast self-renewal. RNAi knockdown of nurf301 or ACF complex components iswi and acf1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G) in the type II neuroblast lineages did not result in any obvious neuroblast overgrowth.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The simultaneous knockdown of both brm and hdac3 under the control of the type II driver resulted in a more severe phenotype of ectopic neuroblasts compared with brm RNAi or hdac3 RNAi knockdown alone.
source: We therefore re-screened the same collection of potential histone modifiers in a brm RNAi background and showed that the simultaneous knockdown of both brm and hdac3 under the control of the type II driver resulted in a more severe phenotype of ectopic neuroblasts (Figure 3D,E; 22.1 ± 7.4 neuroblasts/clone, n = 21) compared with brm RNAi (Figure 3B,E; 10.3 ± 5.6 neuroblasts/clone, n = 30) or hdac3 RNAi knockdown alone (Figure 3C,E; 1.1 ± 0.5 neuroblasts/clone, n = 85).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3B,C,D,E.

claim: HDAC3 functions cooperatively with Brm to regulate type II neuroblast lineages.
source: This finding suggests that HDAC3 functions cooperatively with Brm to regulate type II neuroblast lineages.
evidence: This is inferred from the enhanced phenotype observed when both genes are knocked down simultaneously.

claim: Type II neuroblast MARCM clones from snr16c hdac36c homozygotes possessed a large number of ectopic neuroblasts.
source: Next, we took advantage of an existing deletion mutant snr16c hdac36c, which removes the entire snr1 coding region and the C-terminal region of hdac3. Type II neuroblast MARCM clones from snr16c hdac36c homozygotes possessed a large number of ectopic neuroblasts (Figure 3G,H, 22 ± 11.5 neuroblasts/clone, 83.0%, n = 22).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3G,H.

claim: The number of mature Dpn+ Ase+ INPs in each snr16c hdac36c type II neuroblast clone was modestly reduced compared with control.
source: The number of mature Dpn+ Ase+ INPs in each snr16c hdac36c type II neuroblast clone was modestly reduced to 15.6 ± 4.4 (n = 22) compared with 20.3 ± 3/clone (n = 20) in control, while the number of Dpn− PntP1+ immature and early mature INPs (6.3 ± 3/clone, n = 21) are slightly greater compared with the control clones (4.1 ± 0.9, n = 21).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data from the experiments.

claim: Type I neuroblast clones of snr16c hdac36c double mutant appeared normal, as there was only one neuroblast per clone.
source: In contrast, type I neuroblast clones of this double mutant appeared normal, as there was only one neuroblast per clone (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, n = 17).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Neither type I nor type II neuroblast mutant clones of a loss-of-function hdac3N allele had ectopic neuroblasts.
source: Similar to hdac3 RNAi (Figure 3C), neither type I nor type II neuroblast mutant clones of a loss-of-function hdac3N allele had ectopic neuroblasts (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: HDAC3 acts cooperatively with the Brm complex to suppress the formation of ectopic type II neuroblasts.
source: Our data suggest that HDAC3 acts cooperatively with the Brm complex to suppress the formation of ectopic type II neuroblasts.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from genetic interaction experiments showing enhanced phenotypes.

claim: A significant portion of snr16c hdac36c mutant tissue proliferated massively and formed malignant tumors after transplantation into wild-type hosts.
source: To ascertain whether snr16c hdac36c causes tumorigenesis, larval brain tissues carrying snr16c hdac36c MARCM clones were transplanted into the abdomen of wild-type hosts. A significant portion of the mutant tissue (Figure 3J; 21%, n = 14) proliferated massively and formed malignant tumors, whilst control clones did not proliferate after the implantation (Figure 3I; n = 25).
evidence: This is supported by transplantation experiment data shown in Figure 3I,J.

claim: In subsequent rounds of transplantation, 70% (T1) and 80% (T2) of the snr16c hdac36c mutant brain tissues developed tumors.
source: In subsequent rounds of transplantation, 70% (T1, n = 10) and 80% (T2, n = 5) of the snr16c hdac36c mutant brain tissues developed tumors, suggesting that snr16c hdac36c can induce malignant tumor-like growth after allograft culture.
evidence: This is supported by serial transplantation experiment data.

claim: snr16c hdac36c can induce malignant tumor-like growth after allograft culture.
source: In subsequent rounds of transplantation, 70% (T1, n = 10) and 80% (T2, n = 5) of the snr16c hdac36c mutant brain tissues developed tumors, suggesting that snr16c hdac36c can induce malignant tumor-like growth after allograft culture.
evidence: This is inferred from the serial transplantation results showing sustained tumor growth.

claim: Brm is ubiquitously expressed in various cell types of larval brains, including neuroblasts, INPs, GMCs and neurons.
source: Given that Brm is ubiquitously expressed in various cell types of larval brains, including neuroblasts, INPs, GMCs and neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and data not shown), it is conceivable that the Brm complex may associate with regulatory protein(s) or co-factor(s) that is/are specifically expressed in type II neuroblast lineages to suppress the formation of ectopic neuroblasts.
evidence: This is supported by expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Flag-tagged Brm co-immunoprecipitates with Myc-tagged Erm in S2 cells.
source: Flag-tagged Brm was co-transfected with Myc-tagged Erm in S2 cells. Following immunoprecipitation (IP) of Flag-Brm, Erm can be specifically detected in the immune complex (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Flag-Brm was detected in the immune complex following the IP of Myc-Erm.
source: Consistently, Flag-Brm was detected in the immune complex following the IP of Myc-Erm (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Myc-Brm did not associate with Flag-PntP1 in co-IP experiments.
source: In contrast, Myc-Brm did not associate with Flag-PntP1 in similar co-IP experiments (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that Brm specifically associates in a protein complex with Erm, but not with PntP1.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Brm specifically associates in a protein complex with Erm, but not with PntP1.
source: In contrast, Myc-Brm did not associate with Flag-PntP1 in similar co-IP experiments (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that Brm specifically associates in a protein complex with Erm, but not with PntP1.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential co-IP results with Erm and PntP1.

claim: Myc-Brm associated strongly with Flag-Erm-N and weakly with Flag-Erm-C in co-IP experiments.
source: In co-IP experiments, Myc-Brm associated strongly with Flag-Erm-N and weakly with Flag-Erm-C (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Myc-Brm associated intensely with MBP-Erm-N and weakly with Erm-C, but not with the MBP control in protein pull-down assays.
source: Following the pull-down of amylose resin, Myc-Brm associated intensely with MBP-Erm-N and weakly with Erm-C, but not with the MBP control (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by protein pull-down assay data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Brm physically associates with Erm and Erm N-terminus appears to be more important for this association.
source: These data suggest that Brm physically associates with Erm and Erm N-terminus appears to be more important for this association.
evidence: This is inferred from the stronger association observed with Erm-N compared to Erm-C in both co-IP and pull-down assays.

claim: Flag-BAP60 was detected in the immune complex following IP of Myc-Erm-N but not Myc-Erm-C.
source: In co-IP experiments, Flag-BAP60 was detected in the immune complex following IP of Myc-Erm-N but not Myc-Erm-C (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Myc-Erm-N was detected in the immune complex when IP was performed using Flag-BAP60.
source: Likewise, Myc-Erm-N was detected in the immune complex when IP was performed using Flag-BAP60 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Myc-Snr1 associated with Flag-Erm-N or Flag-Erm-C in co-IP experiments.
source: Moreover, Myc-Snr1 associated with Flag-Erm-N or Flag-Erm-C in co-IP experiments (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Myc-Snr1 associated with MBP-Erm-N and weakly with MBP-Erm-C in protein pull-down assays.
source: Consistently, Myc-Snr1 associated with MBP-Erm-N and weakly with MBP-Erm-C in protein pull-down assays (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by protein pull-down assay data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Several components of the Brm remodeling complex specifically associates with Erm.
source: Therefore, we conclude that the several components of the Brm remodeling complex specifically associates with Erm.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from multiple co-IP and pull-down experiments showing association of Brm, BAP60, and Snr1 with Erm.

claim: Myc-Brm was clearly detected in the immune complex following immunoprecipitation of Flag-HDAC3.
source: Flag-HDAC3 and Myc-Brm were co-transfected in S2 cells. Following immunoprecipitation of Flag-HDAC3, Myc-Brm was clearly detected in the immune complex (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Flag-HDAC3 was detected in the immune complex after IP of Myc-Brm.
source: Similarly, Flag-HDAC3 was detected in the immune complex after IP of Myc-Brm (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: HDAC3 physically associates with Erm-N, but not Erm-C, in both co-IP and protein pull-down assay.
source: Interestingly, HDAC3 also physically associates with Erm-N, but not Erm-C, in both co-IP (Figure 4G) and protein pull-down assay (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation and protein pull-down data shown in Figure 4G,H.

claim: Brm physically associates with Erm and HDAC3 in the protein complex.
source: Taken together, these results show that Brm physically associates with Erm and HDAC3 in the protein complex.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from multiple co-IP and pull-down experiments showing associations among Brm, Erm, and HDAC3.

claim: The simultaneous knockdown of brm and erm resulted in a much more severe phenotype with a large number of ectopic neuroblasts in each lineage compared to brm knockdown alone.
source: The simultaneous knockdown of brm and erm resulted in a much more severe phenotype with a large number of ectopic neuroblasts in each lineage (Figure 5D,E; 37.1 ± 7.6 neuroblasts/lineage, n = 20), in contrast to brm knockdown alone (Figure 5B,E; 9.5 ± 2.8, n = 32).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5B,D,E.

claim: erm RNAi under the type II driver resulted in ectopic type II lineages with each lineage containing one type II neuroblast.
source: Presumably due to incomplete knockdown of erm that only led to weak ectopic type II neuroblasts phenotypes, erm RNAi under the type II driver resulted in ectopic type II lineages with each lineage containing one type II neuroblast (Figure 5C,E; 1 neuroblast/lineage, n = 60).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C,E.

claim: brm and erm genetically interact to prevent the dedifferentiation of INPs back to neuroblasts.
source: This dramatic enhancement suggests that brm and erm genetically interact to prevent the dedifferentiation of INPs back to neuroblasts.
evidence: This is inferred from the enhanced phenotype observed when both genes are knocked down simultaneously.

claim: Knock down of erm by RNAi in the brmT362 MARCM clones significantly enhanced neuroblast overgrowth compared with brmT362 clones.
source: Furthermore, knock down of erm by RNAi in the brmT362 MARCM clones (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B; 9.9 ± 5.5 neuroblasts/clone, n = 32) also significantly enhanced neuroblast overgrowth compared with brmT362 clones (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B; 4.1 ± 2.4 neuroblasts/clone, n = 30).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Overexpression of Erm in type II MARCM clones caused 100% of the neuroblasts to undergo premature differentiation.
source: Similarly, we found that overexpression of Erm in type II MARCM clones caused 100% of the neuroblasts to undergo premature differentiation; 29.3% of the clones contained a neuroblast that gained Ase expression and 41.5% of the clones contained a neuroblast that had gained Ase expression with strongly reduced Dpn expression, while the rest of the clones showed no obvious neuroblasts (Figure 5G and data not shown; n = 41).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The premature differentiation of type II neuroblasts was dramatically suppressed in a brm loss-of-function mutant background when Erm was overexpressed.
source: To assess whether this effect is dependent on its association with Brm, we overexpressed Erm in brm2 type II neuroblast clones. The premature differentiation of type II neuroblasts was dramatically suppressed in a brm loss-of-function mutant background, as there were still 37.8% of clones contained ectopic neuroblasts (Figure 5I), while 62.2% of type II neuroblasts underwent premature differentiation (Figure 5H; n = 37).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H,I.

claim: The simultaneous knockdown of both erm and snr1 resulted in a more severe phenotype of ectopic neuroblasts compared with either erm knockdown or snr1 knockdown.
source: Similarly, the simultaneous knockdown of both erm and snr1 resulted in a more severe phenotype of ectopic neuroblasts (Figure 5M–N; 862 ± 106.8 neuroblasts/brain lobe, n = 20) compared with either erm knockdown (Figure 5K,N; 76.6 ± 14.2 neuroblasts/brain lobe, n = 20) or snr1 knockdown (Figure 5L,N; 219.5 ± 52.2 neuroblasts/brain lobe, n = 20).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5K,L,M,N.

claim: brm and snr1 genetically interact with erm to prevent dedifferentiation of INPs to neuroblasts.
source: Thus, we conclude that brm and snr1 genetically interact with erm to prevent dedifferentiation of INPs to neuroblasts.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from genetic interaction experiments showing enhanced phenotypes.

claim: The simultaneous knockdown of hdac3 and erm under the control of type II driver resulted in a more dramatic increase of ectopic type II neuroblasts compared with either erm knockdown or hdac3 knockdown.
source: Furthermore, the simultaneous knockdown of hdac3 and erm under the control of type II driver also resulted in a more dramatic increase of ectopic type II neuroblasts (Figure 5Q,R; 565.4 ± 68.1 type II neuroblasts/brain lobe, n = 20) compared with either erm knockdown (Figure 5P,R; 76.0 ± 7.7 type II neuroblasts/brain lobe, n = 20) or hdac3 knockdown (Figure 5R; 8 type II neuroblasts/brain lobe, n = 20), suggesting that hdac3 and erm genetically interact in type II neuroblast lineages.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5P,Q,R.

claim: hdac3 and erm genetically interact in type II neuroblast lineages.
source: Furthermore, the simultaneous knockdown of hdac3 and erm under the control of type II driver also resulted in a more dramatic increase of ectopic type II neuroblasts (Figure 5Q,R; 565.4 ± 68.1 type II neuroblasts/brain lobe, n = 20) compared with either erm knockdown (Figure 5P,R; 76.0 ± 7.7 type II neuroblasts/brain lobe, n = 20) or hdac3 knockdown (Figure 5R; 8 type II neuroblasts/brain lobe, n = 20), suggesting that hdac3 and erm genetically interact in type II neuroblast lineages.
evidence: This is inferred from the enhanced phenotype observed when both genes are knocked down simultaneously.

claim: Brm, HDAC3, and Erm function as a repressor complex to prevent INP dedifferentiation into type II neuroblasts.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that Brm, HDAC3, and Erm function as a repressor complex to prevent INP dedifferentiation into type II neuroblasts.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from physical association data and genetic interaction experiments.

claim: The Drosophila Brm remodeling complex displays a tumor suppressor-like function in larval brains.
source: Here, we report a critical function of the Drosophila Brm remodeling complex in suppressing the formation of ectopic type II neuroblasts in larval brains. Mutants of major components of the Brm complex, including Brm and Bap55, and RNAi targeting of several Brm components formed ectopic type II neuroblasts. Therefore, the Drosophila Brm remodeling complex displays a tumor suppressor-like function in larval brains.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that loss of Brm complex components leads to ectopic neuroblasts and tumor formation.

claim: BAP47 (homologous to Snr1) is a bona fide tumor suppressor and the gene is deleted in pediatric rhabdoid tumors.
source: BAP47 (homologous to Snr1) is a bona fide tumor suppressor and the gene is deleted in pediatric rhabdoid tumors (Reisman et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Mutations in epigenetic regulators are found in approximately half of hepatocellular carcinoma and bladder cancers, and represent a significant portion of mutated genes in medulloblastoma.
source: Mutations in epigenetic regulators are found in approximately half of hepatocellular carcinoma and bladder cancers, and represent a significant portion of mutated genes in medulloblastoma (Gui et al., 2011; Fujimoto et al., 2012; Pugh et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous publications.

claim: Drosophila Brm complex is essential for intestinal stem cell proliferation and commitment in the adult intestine.
source: Drosophila Brm complex is essential for intestinal stem cell proliferation and commitment in the adult intestine (Jin et al., 2013; Zeng et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous publications.

claim: Iswi and Domino control germline stem cell and somatic stem cell self-renewal in the ovary.
source: Two other chromatin remodeling factors, Iswi and Domino control germline stem cell and somatic stem cell self-renewal in the ovary (Xi and Xie, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The association with Erm may provide functional specificity of the Brm remodeling complex in type II neuroblast lineages.
source: We speculate that the association with Erm may provide functional specificity of the Brm remodeling complex in type II neuroblast lineages.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the mechanism by which Brm achieves specificity.

claim: 202 sites out of the 270 known genomic loci harboring Brm also contain the de novo Erm DNA-binding motif.
source: Our bioinformatic analysis has identified a 14 bp-long motif as the de novo Erm DNA-binding motif (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–D; and Supplementary methods) and 202 sites out of the 270 known genomic loci harboring Brm (Negre et al., 2011) also contain the de novo Erm DNA-binding motif (Table 2, Gene list).
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis described in the manuscript and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–D.

claim: It is possible that Brm–Erm complex results in a unique configuration of the chromatin 'landscape' in INPs to prevent INP dedifferentiation into neuroblasts.
source: As there are many genes that are potentially co-occupied by Brm and Erm, it is possible that Brm–Erm complex results in a unique configuration of the chromatin 'landscape' in INPs to prevent INP dedifferentiation into neuroblasts.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the mechanism of action.

claim: Disruption of chromatin remodelers may cause widespread changes to the transcriptome, thus amplifying the effect of the single genetic mutation.
source: Therefore, disruption of chromatin remodelers may cause widespread changes to the transcriptome, thus amplifying the effect of the single genetic mutation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the consequences of disrupting chromatin remodelers.

claim: Most class I HDACs are recruited into large multi-subunit co-repressor complexes for maximal activity.
source: Most class I HDACs are recruited into large multi-subunit co-repressor complexes for maximal activity (Wen et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: HDAC1 and 2 are found in multiple co-repressor complexes, while to date HDAC3 appears to be uniquely recruited to the SMRT/N-CoR complex.
source: HDAC1 and 2 are found in multiple co-repressor complexes, while to date HDAC3 appears to be uniquely recruited to the Silencing mediator of retinoic and thyroid receptors (SMRT)/Nuclear receptor co-repressor (N-CoR) complex (Guenther et al., 2000; Li et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous publications.

claim: Drosophila HDAC3 is recruited to a novel multi-subunit complex containing Brm and Erm and that this co–repressor complex prevents dedifferentiation of INPs into type II neuroblasts.
source: Here, we report that Drosophila HDAC3 is recruited to a novel multi-subunit complex containing Brm and Erm and that this co–repressor complex prevents dedifferentiation of INPs into type II neuroblasts.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by physical association and functional data.

claim: The SMRT complex appears not to be important for type II neuroblasts.
source: The SMRT complex appears not to be important for type II neuroblasts, as knockdown of smrter that encodes a core component of the SMRT complex (Heck et al., 2012) neither resulted in any ectopic type II neuroblasts nor enhanced the phenotype of ectopic neuroblasts by brm knockdown (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations that smrter knockdown did not produce relevant phenotypes.

claim: HDAC3 dramatically enhanced the phenotype of ectopic neuroblast upon loss of brm or snr1.
source: We also showed that HDAC3 dramatically enhanced the phenotype of ectopic neuroblast upon loss of brm or snr1, two core components of the Brm complex.
evidence: This is supported by genetic interaction experiments showing enhanced phenotypes.

claim: HDACs are typically recruited by oncogenic protein complexes in lymphoma and leukemia and HDAC3 inhibitors are synergistic or additive with anticancer agents for therapeutics.
source: HDACs are typically recruited by oncogenic protein complexes in lymphoma and leukemia and HDAC3 inhibitors are synergistic or additive with anticancer agents for therapeutics (Dokmanovic et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The finding that HDAC3 functions cooperatively with the Brm complex in suppressing dedifferentiation of INPs into neuroblasts and induces tumors in the allograph transplantation revealed an unexpected potential involvement of HDAC3 in tumor suppression in brain tissue.
source: Our finding that HDAC3 functions cooperatively with the Brm complex in suppressing suppressing dedifferentiation of INPs into neuroblasts and induces tumors in the allograph transplantation revealed an unexpected potential involvement of HDAC3 in tumor suppression in brain tissue.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings showing HDAC3's role in preventing ectopic neuroblasts and tumor formation.

claim: brm knockdown can be partially suppressed by loss of notch.
source: Furthermore, brm knockdown, similar to erm− (Weng et al., 2010), can be partially suppressed by loss of notch (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Simultaneous knockdown of brm and notch in type II neuroblast lineages partially suppressed the ectopic neuroblast phenotype, compared with brm knockdown alone.
source: Simultaneous knockdown of brm and notch in type II neuroblast lineages partially suppressed the ectopic neuroblast phenotype, compared with brm knockdown alone. Type II neuroblast lineages are labeled with Dpn, Ase and CD8.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.
